narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.8). This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle on the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.70 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw this as a clear strength that pulled the prediction toward passing. Your LSAT score of 34 also helped somewhat; although it is a few points below the 37.2 average of accepted applicants, the model still treated it as a modest positive factor.

Unfortunately, the negative impact of your third-year class ranking outweighed the positive effects of your strong GPA and solid LSAT. 

What you should do next is focus on improving your class rank in the remaining law school years and consider a structured bar-preparation program that targets the specific areas where lower-ranked students tend to falter. Raising your standing in future coursework is the most direct way to change this outcome. (218 words)
